title: Static GK
summary: Books and authors, sports, awards, important days, national symbols and firsts, and organisations with their headquarters, currencies and parliaments. These are facts that do not change year to year and add up to 2–4 GA questions in almost every shift. Learn them as tables and review often.

tricks.title: Booker ladder — "Rushdie 81, Roy 97, Desai 06, Adiga 08"
tricks.body: Four India-connected Booker winners in order: **Midnight's Children → God of Small Things → Inheritance of Loss → White Tiger**. **Geetanjali Shree (2022)** won the **International** Booker (for translated fiction).

example.q: Who wrote 'The White Tiger', the 2008 Booker winner?
example.solution: **Aravind Adiga**.

tricks.title: Sports book hooks
tricks.body: **Sunny** Days = **Sunil** Gavaskar · **Race** of My Life = Milkha (the 'Flying Sikh' raced) · **Unbreakable** = Mary Kom (boxer) · **Ace** = Sania (tennis ace) · **Test** of My Life = Yuvraj (cancer battle).

mistakes: *Vande Mataram* is from *Anandamath* (Bankim), **not** from Tagore's works — Tagore wrote *Jana Gana Mana*.
*Unto This Last* was written by **John Ruskin**; Gandhi only paraphrased it into Gujarati as *Sarvodaya*.
*The Discovery of India* was written by **Nehru** in Ahmednagar Fort jail (1942–46).
subtopics.notes:
### Ancient and classical Indian texts
| Book | Author | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Arthashastra** | Kautilya (Chanakya) | Statecraft and economy of the Mauryan age |
| **Rajatarangini** | Kalhana | Historical chronicle of Kashmir |
| **Abhijnana Shakuntalam** | Kalidasa | The most famous Sanskrit drama |
| **Mudrarakshasa** | Vishakhadatta | Story of Chanakya and Chandragupta |
| **Indica** | Megasthenes | Greek envoy's account of Mauryan India |
| **Harshacharita** | Banabhatta | Biography of Harshavardhana |
| **Panchatantra** | Vishnu Sharma | Fable collection |
| **Ramcharitmanas** | Tulsidas | Awadhi retelling of the Ramayana |

### Medieval chronicles and biographies
**Baburnama** - autobiography of Babur (in Turkish, the first of its kind in Indian history); **Akbarnama** and **Ain-i-Akbari** - Abul Fazl; **Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri** - Jahangir's own memoir; **Padshahnama** - Abdul Hamid Lahori (Shah Jahan's reign).

### The freedom era and modern India
| Book | Author |
|---|---|
| **Anandamath** (source of *Vande Mataram*) | Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay |
| **Gitanjali** (Nobel 1913) | Rabindranath Tagore |
| **Hind Swaraj**; **My Experiments with Truth** (autobiography) | M.K. Gandhi |
| **Discovery of India**; **Glimpses of World History** | Jawaharlal Nehru |
| **Poverty and Un-British Rule in India** | Dadabhai Naoroji |
| **Train to Pakistan** | Khushwant Singh |
| **Malgudi Days**; **Swami and Friends** | R.K. Narayan |
| **A Suitable Boy** | Vikram Seth |

### Autobiographies and memoirs
**Wings of Fire** - A.P.J. Abdul Kalam; **Long Walk to Freedom** - Nelson Mandela; **The Story of My Life** - Helen Keller; **Autobiography of an Unknown Indian** - Nirad C. Chaudhuri; **Playing It My Way** - Sachin Tendulkar; **Straight from the Heart** - Kapil Dev; **A Shot at History** - Abhinav Bindra.

### Indian winners of the Booker Prize
**Midnight's Children** - Salman Rushdie (1981; also the 'Booker of Bookers'); **The God of Small Things** - Arundhati Roy (1997); **The Inheritance of Loss** - Kiran Desai (2006); **The White Tiger** - Aravind Adiga (2008). Kiran Desai is the daughter of Anita Desai, who was shortlisted several times but never won.

### World classics in one glance
| Book | Author | Book | Author |
|---|---|---|---|
| War and Peace | Tolstoy | Crime and Punishment | Dostoevsky |
| Pride and Prejudice | Jane Austen | Hamlet, Macbeth | Shakespeare |
| Iliad, Odyssey | Homer | Don Quixote | Cervantes |
| One Hundred Years of Solitude | Marquez | The Old Man and the Sea | Hemingway |
| Animal Farm, 1984 | Orwell | The Godfather | Puzo |
| The Origin of Species | Darwin | Das Kapital | Karl Marx |
| The Wealth of Nations | Adam Smith | The Republic | Plato |
| Paradise Lost | Milton | The Canterbury Tales | Chaucer |

### Quick revision
- Kautilya-Arthashastra, Kalhana-Rajatarangini, Kalidasa-Shakuntalam, Megasthenes-Indica, Banabhatta-Harshacharita, Vishnu Sharma-Panchatantra.
- Baburnama = Babur's own story; Akbarnama = Abul Fazl; Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri = Jahangir.
- Gandhi-Hind Swaraj + My Experiments with Truth; Nehru-Discovery of India; Tagore-Gitanjali (Nobel 1913).
- Bookers: Rushdie 1981, Roy 1997, Kiran Desai 2006, Adiga 2008.
- Wings of Fire-Kalam, Long Walk to Freedom-Mandela, Playing It My Way-Tendulkar.

patterns.name: Ancient/medieval text ↔ author
patterns.howToSpot: 'Who wrote Arthashastra/Rajatarangini/Akbarnama', 'Indica is an account of', Sanskrit drama questions.
patterns.logic:
1. Ancient set: Kautilya-Arthashastra, Kalhana-Rajatarangini, Kalidasa-Abhijnana Shakuntalam, Vishakhadatta-Mudrarakshasa, Megasthenes-Indica, Banabhatta-Harshacharita, Vishnu Sharma-Panchatantra.
2. Mughal set: Babur-Baburnama (own memoir), Abul Fazl-Akbarnama + Ain-i-Akbari, Jahangir-Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri.
3. Distractors usually swap authors within the same period - eliminate by court and century.

example.q: Who wrote **Rajatarangini**, the historical chronicle of Kashmir?
example.solution: **Kalhana** (12th century). Arthashastra - Kautilya; Harshacharita - Banabhatta.

patterns.name: Freedom-era work ↔ author
patterns.howToSpot: 'Discovery of India was written by', 'Hind Swaraj', 'Anandamath', 'Gitanjali', works of Gandhi-Nehru-Tagore-Bankim.
patterns.logic:
1. Gandhi - **Hind Swaraj** and his autobiography **My Experiments with Truth**; Nehru - **Discovery of India** and **Glimpses of World History**.
2. Bankim Chandra - **Anandamath** (source of *Vande Mataram*); Tagore - **Gitanjali** (Nobel 1913).
3. Dadabhai Naoroji - **Poverty and Un-British Rule in India** (drain theory).

example.q: **Anandamath**, the novel that gave the nation *Vande Mataram*, was written by —
example.solution: **Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay**. Discovery of India - Nehru; Hind Swaraj - Gandhi.

patterns.name: Autobiography ↔ author
patterns.howToSpot: 'Wings of Fire is the autobiography of', 'Long Walk to Freedom', 'My Experiments with Truth', memoir matching.
patterns.logic:
1. **Wings of Fire** - A.P.J. Abdul Kalam; **My Experiments with Truth** - M.K. Gandhi; **Long Walk to Freedom** - Nelson Mandela.
2. **Playing It My Way** - Sachin Tendulkar; **A Shot at History** - Abhinav Bindra; **The Story of My Life** - Helen Keller.
3. **Baburnama** is the earliest autobiography linked to India - Babur's own, in Turkish.

example.q: **Long Walk to Freedom** is the autobiography of —
example.solution: **Nelson Mandela**. Wings of Fire - Kalam; My Experiments with Truth - Gandhi.

patterns.name: Booker Prize winners ↔ book
patterns.howToSpot: 'Who wrote The White Tiger', 'Midnight's Children', 'The Inheritance of Loss', Booker-linking questions.
patterns.logic:
1. Indian Booker winners: **Midnight's Children - Salman Rushdie (1981)**, **The God of Small Things - Arundhati Roy (1997)**, **The Inheritance of Loss - Kiran Desai (2006)**, **The White Tiger - Aravind Adiga (2008)**.
2. Midnight's Children also won the 'Booker of Bookers'.
3. Anita Desai was repeatedly shortlisted but never won - a favourite distractor next to her daughter Kiran.

example.q: Who is the author of **The White Tiger** (Booker Prize 2008)?
example.solution: **Aravind Adiga**. The other Indian Booker books: Midnight's Children-Rushdie, God of Small Things-Roy, Inheritance of Loss-Kiran Desai.

patterns.name: World classic ↔ author
patterns.howToSpot: 'War and Peace', 'One Hundred Years of Solitude', 'Don Quixote', 'The Republic', foreign classics and thinkers.
patterns.logic:
1. Russia: Tolstoy-War and Peace, Dostoevsky-Crime and Punishment.

example.q: **One Hundred Years of Solitude**, a landmark of magical realism, was written by —
example.solution: **Gabriel Garcia Marquez** (Colombia). Don Quixote - Cervantes; War and Peace - Tolstoy.

**Players per side**

| 5 | 6 | 7 | 9 | 11 | 15 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Basketball | Volleyball, ice hockey | Kabaddi, netball, water polo, handball | Kho-kho (in field), baseball | Cricket, football, hockey | Rugby union |

**Terms → sport**: *Googly, LBW, maiden over* → cricket · *Bully, penalty corner* → hockey · *Love, deuce, ace* → tennis · *Checkmate, castling, en passant* → chess · *Smash, drop shot* → badminton · *Birdie, bogey, caddie* → golf · *Raid, bonus line* → kabaddi · *Punch, knock-out, uppercut* → boxing.

**Grand Slam surfaces:** Australian Open (hard, Jan) · **French Open / Roland Garros (clay)** · **Wimbledon (grass)** · US Open (hard, Flushing Meadows).

**Olympics essentials**
- Paris **2024** (India: 6 medals — Neeraj Chopra silver; **Manu Bhaker** two bronzes, the first Indian after independence to win two medals at one Games).
- Los Angeles **2028**, Brisbane **2032**.
- **Abhinav Bindra** — India's first individual Olympic gold (**Beijing 2008**, 10 m air rifle).
- **Neeraj Chopra** — javelin gold, Tokyo 2020 (India's first in athletics).
- Olympic rings: 5 (blue, yellow, black, green, red) = 5 continents.

**Indian stadiums:** Eden Gardens (Kolkata) · Narendra Modi Stadium (Motera, Ahmedabad — world's largest cricket stadium) · Wankhede (Mumbai) · Chepauk / M.A. Chidambaram (Chennai) · Salt Lake / Vivekananda Yuba Bharati Krirangan (Kolkata, football) · Major Dhyan Chand National Stadium (Delhi, hockey).

tricks.title: Badminton cups — "Thomas the man, Uber the woman"
tricks.body: **Thomas** Cup = men's team, **Uber** Cup = women's team, **Sudirman** = mixed. Tennis: **D**avis = **D**udes (men), **B**illie Jean King = women.

example.q: India won the Thomas Cup for the first time in 2022. The sport is —
example.solution: **Badminton** (men's team championship).

tricks.title: Team size — "Basket 5, Volley 6, Kabaddi 7"
tricks.body: Count up: basketball **5**, volleyball **6**, kabaddi **7**; then cricket/football/hockey **11**.

mistakes: Santosh Trophy is **football**; Ranji Trophy is **cricket**.
Roland Garros is **clay**; Wimbledon is the only Grand Slam on **grass**.
Abhinav Bindra won India's first **individual** gold; India had team golds in hockey much earlier (from 1928).
subtopics.notes:
### Trophy or cup → sport (the classic match-the-column)
| Trophy | Sport | Trophy | Sport |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ranji, Duleep, Irani, Deodhar, Vijay Hazare | Cricket (India) | The Ashes | Cricket (England v Australia) |
| Santosh Trophy | Football (states) | Durand Cup | Football (oldest in India, 1888) |
| Aga Khan, Beighton Cup | Hockey | Rangaswami Cup | Hockey (national championship) |
| Sultan Azlan Shah Cup | Hockey (Malaysia) | Thomas Cup | Badminton (men) |
| Uber Cup | Badminton (women) | Sudirman Cup | Badminton (mixed) |
| Davis Cup | Tennis (men) | Billie Jean King Cup | Tennis (women) |
| Ryder Cup | Golf | Swaythling Cup | Table tennis (men) |
| Ezra Cup | Polo | Ballon d'Or | Football (best player award) |

### Terms → sport
Hockey: **bully, penalty corner, dribble, scoop**. Cricket: **googly, yorker, LBW, gully, cover drive**. Golf: **birdie, eagle, bogey, caddie, tee**. Chess: **gambit, stalemate, castling, checkmate**. Tennis: **deuce, ace, love, smash, volley**. Shooting: **bull's eye**. Volleyball: **spike, blocking**. 'Love' and 'deuce' belong to both tennis and badminton scoring.

### Players per side
Cricket 11 - Football 11 - Hockey 11 - Rugby union 15 - Kabaddi **7** - Kho-kho **9** - Volleyball **6** - Basketball **5** - Water polo **7** - Baseball **9** - Polo **4**.

### Grand Slams and big tournaments
Four tennis Grand Slams: **Australian Open (hard)** - **French Open / Roland Garros (clay)** - **Wimbledon (grass, oldest, since 1877)** - **US Open (hard)**. Football's FIFA World Cup: first in **1930 (Uruguay)**, held every four years. Cricket World Cup: first in **1975 (England; West Indies won)**.

### The Olympics
| Fact | Answer |
|---|---|
| First modern Olympics | **1896, Athens** (revived by **Pierre de Coubertin**; IOC founded 1894, Paris) |
| Motto | **Citius, Altius, Fortius** (Faster, Higher, Stronger - 'Communiter'/Together added 2021) |
| Five rings | Unity of the **five continents**; designed by Coubertin |
| Marathon | **42.195 km** |
| India's first Olympic appearance | 1900 Paris - **Norman Pritchard** won two athletics silvers |
| First hockey gold | **1928 Amsterdam** (first of 8) |
| First individual medal | **K.D. Jadhav**, wrestling, 1952 Helsinki |
| First individual gold | **Abhinav Bindra**, 10 m air rifle shooting, 2008 Beijing |
| Second individual gold | **Neeraj Chopra**, javelin (87.58 m), Tokyo 2020 |
Other milestones: **Viswanathan Anand** became India's first chess Grandmaster in 1988; the **Ranji Trophy** began in 1934.

### Quick revision
- Cricket: Ranji-Duleep-Irani; Ashes = England v Australia; first Cricket WC 1975.
- Football: Santosh (states), Durand (1888), FIFA WC 1930 Uruguay.
- Badminton: Thomas men, Uber women, Sudirman mixed; Tennis: Davis men, BJK women.
- Team sizes: kabaddi 7, kho-kho 9, polo 4, basketball 5, volleyball 6, rugby 15.
- Olympics: 1896 Athens, Coubertin, 42.195 km, Pritchard 1900, Jadhav 1952, Bindra 2008, Neeraj 2020.

patterns.name: Trophy / cup ↔ sport
patterns.howToSpot: 'Santosh/Durand/Thomas/Davis/Ryder trophy is associated with', match-the-column on cups.
patterns.logic:
1. Cricket: Ranji, Duleep, Irani, Deodhar, Vijay Hazare; the **Ashes** = England v Australia.
2. Football: **Santosh** (states of India), **Durand** (oldest Indian tournament, 1888), Ballon d'Or (player award). Hockey: Aga Khan, Beighton, Rangaswami, Sultan Azlan Shah.
3. Rackets: **Thomas (men) / Uber (women) / Sudirman (mixed)** in badminton; **Davis (men) / Billie Jean King (women)** in tennis; **Ryder Cup** = golf; **Swaythling Cup** = table tennis; **Ezra Cup** = polo.

example.q: The **Durand Cup**, the oldest football tournament of India, was first played in —
example.solution: **1888** at Shimla - older than the FIFA World Cup by 42 years; the Santosh Trophy is the national championship for states.

patterns.name: Sporting term ↔ sport
patterns.howToSpot: 'Googly/yorker belong to', 'gambit/checkmate', 'deuce/ace/love', 'bull's eye', term matching.
patterns.logic:
1. Cricket: googly, yorker, LBW, gully, cover drive, silly point.
2. Hockey: bully, penalty corner, dribble, scoop. Tennis: deuce, ace, love, smash, volley; badminton shares love and smash.
3. Golf: birdie, eagle, bogey, caddie, tee; Chess: gambit, castling, stalemate, checkmate; Shooting: bull's eye.

example.q: The terms '**googly**' and '**yorker**' are associated with which sport?
example.solution: **Cricket**. Bully and penalty corner belong to hockey; birdie and bogey to golf.

patterns.name: Number of players per side
patterns.howToSpot: 'How many players in a kabaddi/water polo/polo team', team-size ordering questions.
patterns.logic:
1. Eleven: cricket, football, hockey. Fifteen: rugby union.
2. Smaller sides: kabaddi **7**, kho-kho **9**, volleyball **6**, basketball **5**, water polo **7**, baseball **9**, polo **4**.
3. Recall the odd ones - polo 4, kabaddi 7, rugby 15 - the rest sit in a narrow band.

example.q: How many players does a **kabaddi** team field on the mat?
example.solution: **Seven**. Kho-kho fields nine; basketball five; volleyball six.

patterns.name: Grand Slams and major tournaments ↔ surface / venue
patterns.howToSpot: 'Which Grand Slam is played on grass/clay', 'oldest tennis tournament', 'Wimbledon is played at'.
patterns.logic:
1. Order of the year: Australian Open (hard) - **Roland Garros** (clay) - **Wimbledon** (grass) - US Open (hard).
2. Wimbledon is the oldest (since 1877) and played at the All England Club, London.
3. First FIFA World Cup - **1930, Uruguay**; first Cricket World Cup - **1975, England**.

example.q: The **Australian Open** and the **US Open** are played on which type of surface?
example.solution: **Hard courts**. The French Open (Roland Garros) is on clay and Wimbledon on grass.

patterns.name: Olympics: history, symbols and India's milestones
patterns.howToSpot: 'First modern Olympics', 'Olympic motto', 'five rings represent', 'first Indian individual medal/gold', marathon distance.
patterns.logic:
1. First modern Olympics - **1896, Athens**; revived by **Baron Pierre de Coubertin**; IOC founded 1894 (Paris).
2. Motto - **Citius, Altius, Fortius** ('Together' added 2021); five rings = five continents; marathon = **42.195 km**.
3. India: Norman Pritchard 1900 (two silvers); hockey gold from **1928 Amsterdam** (8 in all); K.D. Jadhav 1952 first individual medal; **Abhinav Bindra 2008** first individual gold; **Neeraj Chopra Tokyo 2020** javelin gold (87.58 m).

example.q: The five interlocking rings of the Olympic flag represent —
example.solution: The **five continents** of the world united by sport; the rings were designed by Coubertin and first flown in 1920.

**Indian Nobel laureates**

|---|---|---|

example.q: Which of the following was NOT among the first Bharat Ratna recipients in 1954? (a) C.V. Raman (b) S. Radhakrishnan (c) Jawaharlal Nehru (d) C. Rajagopalachari
example.solution: **Nehru** (awarded 1955). 1954 = RRR.

tricks.title: Award decade ladder
tricks.body: **50s** Bharat Ratna (54) → **60s** Arjuna (61), Jnanpith (65), Phalke (69) → **80s** Dronacharya (85) → **90s** Khel Ratna (91–92).

mistakes: Dronacharya is for **coaches**; Arjuna is for **players**.
The first Phalke awardee was **Devika Rani**, not Prithviraj Kapoor (he got it posthumously in 1971).
Khel Ratna was **renamed** after Major Dhyan Chand in 2021; the separate *Dhyan Chand Award* (lifetime) is a different award.
subtopics.notes:
### Civilian awards of India (in order of precedence)
**Bharat Ratna > Padma Vibhushan > Padma Bhushan > Padma Shri.** All four were instituted in **1954**. Bharat Ratna facts: first recipients (1954) - **C. Rajagopalachari, S. Radhakrishnan, C.V. Raman**; first woman - **Indira Gandhi (1971)**; first awarded posthumously - **Lal Bahadur Shastri (1966)**; first (and youngest) sportsperson - **Sachin Tendulkar (2014)**.

### Gallantry awards
**Param Vir Chakra (PVC)** - the highest wartime gallantry award (its peacetime counterpart is the **Ashoka Chakra**). The **first PVC went posthumously to Major Somnath Sharma** (1947, Kashmir operations). Below it come the Maha Vir Chakra and the Vir Chakra.

### Nobel Prizes (from 1901)
Categories: Physics, Chemistry, Medicine, Literature, Peace (Economics added in 1969 by Sweden's central bank, not by Nobel's will). Indians and people of Indian origin:
| Person | Year | Field |
|---|---|---|
| **Rabindranath Tagore** | 1913 | Literature (first Asian) |
| **C.V. Raman** | 1930 | Physics |
| **Mother Teresa** | 1979 | Peace |
| **Hargobind Khorana** | 1968 | Medicine |
| **Amartya Sen** | 1998 | Economics |
| **V. Ramakrishnan** | 2009 | Chemistry |
| **Kailash Satyarthi** | 2014 | Peace (with Malala Yousafzai) |
| **Abhijit Banerjee** | 2019 | Economics |
**Marie Curie** was the first woman Nobel laureate (Physics 1903) and the only one to win in two sciences (Chemistry 1911).

### Literary, arts and other international awards
- **Jnanpith Award** (1965) - India's highest literary award; first winner **G. Sankara Kurup** (Malayalam).
- **Dadasaheb Phalke Award** (1969) - India's highest cinema honour; first winner **Devika Rani**.
- **Booker Prize** - first awarded 1969 to P.H. Newby; **Pulitzer Prize** (1917) - American journalism and letters.
- **Ramon Magsaysay Award** (1958) - the 'Asian Nobel'; named after a Philippine president.
- **Gandhi Peace Prize** (1995) - instituted by India; first won by **Julius Nyerere** of Tanzania.
- **Abel Prize** (2003, Norway) - mathematics; **Fields Medal** - mathematics, for work done under 40, every four years; **Turing Award** - computer science.

### Sports awards of India
**Major Dhyan Chand Khel Ratna** - India's highest sporting honour (first given 1991-92 to **Viswanathan Anand**; renamed from Rajiv Gandhi Khel Ratna in 2021). **Dronacharya Award** (1985) - outstanding **coaches**. **Arjuna Award** (1961) - consistent outstanding sportspersons. **Dhyan Chand Award** - lifetime achievement. **Maulana Abul Kalam Azad (MAKA) Trophy** - best university in sports.

### Quick revision
- 1954: Bharat Ratna + three Padma awards; first Bharat Ratna trio Rajagopalachari-Radhakrishnan-Raman.
- PVC first = Major Somnath Sharma (posthumous); peacetime equivalent = Ashoka Chakra.
- Nobel ladder: Tagore 1913, Khorana 1968, Raman 1930, Mother Teresa 1979, Sen 1998, Ramakrishnan 2009, Satyarthi 2014, Banerjee 2019.
- Jnanpith 1965 Kurup; Phalke 1969 Devika Rani; Magsaysay 1958; Gandhi Peace Prize 1995 Nyerere.
- Khel Ratna first = Anand (1991-92); Dronacharya = coaches; Arjuna = players.

subtopics.notes:
### National symbols of India
| Symbol | Identity |
|---|---|
| **Tiger** | National animal |
| **Peacock** | National bird (declared 1963) |
| **Lotus** | National flower |
| **Banyan** | National tree |
| **Mango** | National fruit |
| **Ganga** | National river (2008) |
| **Gangetic river dolphin** | National aquatic animal (2009) |
| **Elephant** | National heritage animal (2010) |
| **Saka calendar** | National calendar (used with the Gregorian since 1957) |
| **Gazette of India** | Official gazette |

### The flag
Designed on the lines suggested by **Pingali Venkayya**; adopted on **22 July 1947**; ratio **3 : 2**; a navy-blue **24-spoke Ashoka Chakra** at the centre (taken from the Sarnath Lion Capital). Saffron - courage and sacrifice; white - truth and peace; green - faith and prosperity. The Flag Code of India was liberalised in 2002 (and further in 2021) to let the public hoist the flag.

### Emblem, anthem and song
**State Emblem**: adapted from the **Lion Capital of Ashoka at Sarnath**, adopted on **26 January 1950**; motto **Satyameva Jayate** ('truth alone triumphs'), from the **Mundaka Upanishad**. **National anthem** - *Jana Gana Mana* by **Tagore**, adopted **24 January 1950** (playing time about 52 seconds). **National song** - *Vande Mataram* by **Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay** (from *Anandamath*), first sung at the 1896 Congress session.

### Firsts - women
| First | Person |
|---|---|
| First woman Governor of a state | **Sarojini Naidu** (UP, 1947) |
| First woman Chief Minister | **Sucheta Kripalani** (UP, 1963) |
| First woman President of India | **Pratibha Patil** (2007) |
| First woman Speaker of the Lok Sabha | **Meira Kumar** (2009) |
| First woman IPS officer | **Kiran Bedi** (1972) |
| First Indian woman in space | **Kalpana Chawla** (1997) |
| First Indian woman to climb Everest | **Bachendri Pal** (1984) |
| First woman President of the INC | Annie Besant (1917); Sarojini Naidu the first Indian woman (1925) |

### Firsts - the pioneering list
**First President** - Rajendra Prasad (1950; longest-serving); **first Prime Minister** - Jawaharlal Nehru (longest-serving); **first Field Marshal** - Sam Manekshaw (1973); **first Indian in space** - Rakesh Sharma (1984, Soviet Soyuz T-11); **first Indian Nobel laureate** - Tagore (1913). Science and infrastructure: first feature film **Raja Harishchandra** (1913, Dadasaheb Phalke); first satellite **Aryabhata** (1975); Mars orbiter **Mangalyaan** (2013); **Chandrayaan-3** soft-landed near the lunar south pole on **23 August 2023**, now observed as **National Space Day**. First passenger railway - **Bombay to Thane, 16 April 1853**; first census - 1872 (regular from 1881); first Five-Year Plan - 1951; first bank - Bank of Hindustan (1770).

### Quick revision
- Tiger-peacock-lotus-banyan-mango-Ganga-Gangetic dolphin-elephant-Saka calendar.
- Flag: Venkayya design, 22 July 1947, 3:2, 24 spokes; emblem: Sarnath, 26 Jan 1950, Mundaka Upanishad.
- Anthem adopted 24 Jan 1950 (Tagore); Vande Mataram = Bankim Chandra, Anandamath.
- Women firsts: Naidu (Governor), Kripalani (CM), Patil (President), Bedi (IPS), Chawla (space), Pal (Everest).
- Manekshaw 1973 Field Marshal; Rakesh Sharma 1984; Aryabhata 1975; Chandrayaan-3 = 23 Aug = National Space Day; railway 1853.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Who wrote X', 'X is the autobiography of', 'the Booker-winning novel X was written by', match-the-column of books and authors.
pyqPatterns.approach: Split your revision into four racks: ancient/medieval texts (Kautilya, Kalhana, Kalidasa, Abul Fazl), freedom-era works (Gandhi, Nehru, Tagore, Bankim), autobiographies (Wings of Fire, Long Walk to Freedom, Playing It My Way) and Booker winners (Rushdie 1981, Roy 1997, Kiran Desai 2006, Adiga 2008). In match-the-column, strike options whose author belongs to another rack.

example.q: Who is the author of **The Discovery of India**?
example.solution: **Jawaharlal Nehru**, written during imprisonment in 1942-46; his other work is Glimpses of World History.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Santosh/Thomas/Davis/Ryder trophy is associated with', 'googly/gambit/deuce belong to', 'how many players in a team of X'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Keep three lists: trophies by sport (cricket - Ranji and Ashes; football - Santosh and Durand; badminton - Thomas/Uber/Sudirman; tennis - Davis/Billie Jean King; golf - Ryder), terms by sport (bully-hockey, googly-cricket, birdie-golf, gambit-chess, deuce-tennis, bull's eye-shooting) and the odd team sizes (polo 4, basketball 5, volleyball 6, kabaddi/water polo 7, kho-kho 9, rugby 15).

example.q: The **Thomas Cup** is associated with which sport?
example.solution: **Badminton** - the world men's team championship; the Uber Cup is its women's counterpart.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'First Bharat Ratna/Nobel/Param Vir Chakra', 'which award is given for coaching', 'Abel/Fields/Turing are given for', 'first recipient of X award'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Anchor each award to its first and its field: Bharat Ratna 1954 (trio Rajagopalachari-Radhakrishnan-Raman), Nobel ladder (Tagore 1913 first), PVC first Major Somnath Sharma, Jnanpith 1965 Kurup, Phalke 1969 Devika Rani, Khel Ratna first Anand. Fields: Abel-Fields = mathematics, Turing = computing, Dronacharya = coaches, Arjuna = players.

example.q: The **Dronacharya Award** honours —
example.solution: Outstanding **coaches** who produce medal-winners; the Arjuna Award goes to sportspersons themselves.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Which day falls on 5 September', 'World Environment Day date', 'National Sports Day honours', calendar-matching questions.
pyqPatterns.approach: Two mini-tables settle everything. Person-linked dates: 12 Jan Vivekananda, 1 Jul B.C. Roy, 29 Aug Dhyan Chand, 5 Sep Radhakrishnan, 15 Sep Visvesvaraya, 14 Nov Nehru, 22 Dec Ramanujan. International dates: 22 Mar Water, 7 Apr Health (WHO 1948), 22 Apr Earth, 5 Jun Environment, 21 Jun Yoga, 16 Oct Food (FAO), 24 Oct UN, 10 Dec Human Rights (UDHR).

example.q: **World Environment Day** is observed on —
example.solution: **5 June** - the date the Stockholm Conference began in 1972; Earth Day is 22 April.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Where is NATO/ADB/INTERPOL headquartered', 'currency of X', 'Knesset/Diet is the parliament of', 'national aquatic animal/heritage animal'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Group by city for HQs (New York - UN/UNICEF; Geneva - WHO/WTO/ILO; Paris - UNESCO; Rome - FAO; Nairobi - UNEP; Vienna - IAEA/OPEC; The Hague - ICJ; Brussels - NATO; Kathmandu - SAARC; Manila - ADB; Dubai - ICC; Lausanne - IOC; Lyon - INTERPOL) and by country for currencies (taka, ngultrum, kyat, baht, rand, real) and parliaments (Knesset-Israel, Diet-Japan, Majlis-Iran, Bundestag-Germany, Duma-Russia, Folketing-Denmark, Storting-Norway).

example.q: The headquarters of the **International Cricket Council (ICC)** are in —
example.solution: **Dubai** (UAE); the ICC moved from Lord's, London, in 2005.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'First modern Olympics', 'Olympic motto/rings', 'first FIFA/Cricket World Cup', 'India's first individual gold', marathon distance.
pyqPatterns.approach: One Olympics card: 1896 Athens (Coubertin, IOC 1894), motto Citius-Altius-Fortius, five rings = five continents, marathon 42.195 km; India - Pritchard 1900, hockey gold 1928, Jadhav 1952 first individual medal, Bindra 2008 first individual gold, Neeraj Chopra 2020. Tournaments: first FIFA World Cup 1930 (Uruguay), first Cricket World Cup 1975 (England; West Indies won), Ranji Trophy 1934.

example.q: In which year was the **first Cricket World Cup** played?
example.solution: **1975** - hosted by England and won by the West Indies (India's first title came in 1983).

example.q: Who was India's **first woman IPS officer**?
example.solution: **Kiran Bedi** (joined the service in 1972).

solvedExamples.q: Which of the following pairs of book and author is **NOT** correctly matched?
options: India Wins Freedom — Maulana Abul Kalam Azad
The Discovery of India — Jawaharlal Nehru
solvedExamples.solution: *Hind Swaraj* (1909) was written by **M.K. Gandhi** on board a ship from London to South Africa. Tilak's famous works are *Gita Rahasya* and *The Arctic Home in the Vedas*. The other pairs are correct.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Hind Swaraj = Gandhi's first manifesto; Tilak = Gita Rahasya.

solvedExamples.q: How many players does each side have on court in a game of **volleyball**?
solvedExamples.solution: Volleyball is played **6-a-side**. Basketball has 5, kabaddi 7 and baseball/kho-kho 9.

solvedExamples.q: Who was the first recipient of the **Dadasaheb Phalke Award**, instituted in 1969?
solvedExamples.solution: Actress **Devika Rani** ('First Lady of Indian Cinema') received the first Phalke Award for 1969. Prithviraj Kapoor received it posthumously (1971), Raj Kapoor in 1987 and Satyajit Ray in 1984.
solvedExamples.shortcut: First Phalke = the First Lady of Indian cinema.

solvedExamples.q:
Match the organisations with their headquarters and choose the correct option.

A. UNESCO  B. UNEP  C. IAEA

1. Vienna  2. Paris  3. Nairobi
solvedExamples.solution: **UNESCO – Paris**, **UNEP – Nairobi**, **IAEA – Vienna** (also home to OPEC).
solvedExamples.shortcut: Fix UNESCO = Paris first — only option (a) and (c) have A-2; then UNEP = Nairobi settles it.

practice.q: The novel ***Godan*** was written by —
practice.solution: ***Godan*** (1936), Premchand's last completed novel, tells the story of the poor farmer Hori. Premchand also wrote *Gaban* and *Nirmala*.

practice.q: ***The God of Small Things***, winner of the 1997 Booker Prize, was written by —
practice.solution: **Arundhati Roy** won the Booker in **1997** for this Kerala-set debut novel. Kiran Desai won in 2006 for *The Inheritance of Loss*.

practice.q: ***Playing It My Way*** is the autobiography of —
practice.solution: ***Playing It My Way*** (2014) is **Sachin Tendulkar**'s autobiography, written with Boria Majumdar.
practice.shortcut: Sachin — 'my way' of playing for 24 years.

practice.q: ***Poverty and Un-British Rule in India***, which set out the 'drain of wealth' theory, was written by —
practice.solution: **Dadabhai Naoroji**, the 'Grand Old Man of India', published this book in 1901. R.C. Dutt wrote *The Economic History of India*.

practice.q: The **Santosh Trophy** is associated with —
practice.solution: The **Santosh Trophy** is India's national football championship for state teams, first held in 1941. The Ranji Trophy is its cricket counterpart.

practice.q: The **Uber Cup** is a world team championship for —
practice.solution: The **Uber Cup** is the women's world team badminton championship. The **Thomas Cup** is its men's version.

practice.q: The terms '**bully**' and '**penalty corner**' are associated with —
practice.solution: Both terms belong to **field hockey** — a bully restarts play between two players, and a penalty corner is awarded for defensive fouls inside the circle.
practice.shortcut: Penalty **corner** + bully = hockey (football has corner kicks, not penalty corners).

practice.q: Which Grand Slam tennis tournament is played on **clay courts**?
practice.solution: The **French Open** at Roland Garros, Paris is the only Grand Slam on **clay**. Wimbledon is on grass; the Australian and US Opens are on hard courts.

practice.q: Which shooter won India's **first individual Olympic gold medal**?
practice.solution: **Abhinav Bindra** won the **10 m air rifle** gold at **Beijing 2008**. Rathore won silver in 2004 (double trap); Narang and Vijay Kumar won medals in 2012.

practice.q: Which of the following received the **Bharat Ratna in 1954**, the first year of the award?
practice.solution: The 1954 recipients were **C. Rajagopalachari, S. Radhakrishnan and C.V. Raman**. Nehru got it in 1955; Ambedkar and Patel received it posthumously in 1990 and 1991.

practice.q: The **Dronacharya Award** is given for excellence in —
practice.solution: Instituted in **1985**, the Dronacharya Award honours **sports coaches**. The Arjuna Award is for sportspersons.
practice.shortcut: Drona was the guru (coach) of Arjuna — coach vs player.

practice.q: The first **Jnanpith Award** (1965) went to G. Sankara Kurup, who wrote in —
practice.solution: **G. Sankara Kurup** received the first Jnanpith for his **Malayalam** poetry collection *Odakkuzhal* ('The Bamboo Flute').

practice.q: **National Science Day** is celebrated in India on —
practice.solution: **28 February** marks C.V. Raman's discovery of the **Raman effect** in 1928. 7 November is Raman's birthday; 11 May is National Technology Day (Pokhran-II, 1998); 15 September is Engineers' Day.
practice.shortcut: Science Day = discovery date, not birthday.

practice.q: **National Sports Day** (29 August) is observed on the birth anniversary of —
practice.solution: Hockey wizard **Major Dhyan Chand** was born on 29 August 1905. The Khel Ratna is also named after him (since 2021).

practice.q: Who was the **first woman Governor** of an Indian state?
practice.solution: **Sarojini Naidu** became Governor of the United Provinces (now UP) in 1947. Sucheta Kriplani was the first woman Chief Minister (UP, 1963). Her daughter Padmaja Naidu later governed West Bengal.

practice.q: The motto '**Satyameva Jayate**' on India's national emblem is taken from the —
practice.solution: The words come from the **Mundaka Upanishad** ('Truth alone triumphs'). The emblem itself is adapted from Ashoka's Lion Capital at Sarnath.

practice.q: The currency of **Bhutan** is the —
practice.solution: Bhutan's currency is the **Ngultrum**, pegged at par with the Indian rupee. Taka = Bangladesh, Kyat = Myanmar, Rupiah = Indonesia.

practice.q: The headquarters of the **International Labour Organization (ILO)** is in —
practice.solution: The ILO, founded in **1919**, is based in **Geneva**, along with WHO and WTO.

practice.q: The **Knesset** is the parliament of —
practice.solution: The **Knesset** is Israel's unicameral legislature in Jerusalem. Iran – Majlis, Japan – Diet, Norway – Storting.

practice.q: The **Arthashastra**, the ancient treatise on statecraft, is attributed to:
practice.solution: **Kautilya (Chanakya)**, minister of Chandragupta Maurya, wrote the Arthashastra on polity, economy and spy-craft.

practice.q: **Indica**, an account of Mauryan India by a Greek envoy, was written by:
practice.solution: **Megasthenes**, ambassador of Seleucus Nicator at Chandragupta Maurya's court, wrote **Indica**; the original is lost but quoted by later writers.

practice.q: The **Harshacharita**, a biography of Emperor Harshavardhana, was composed by:
practice.solution: **Banabhatta**, Harsha's court poet, wrote the **Harshacharita** (and the prose romance Kadambari).

practice.q: Which Mughal emperor wrote his own memoir, the **Baburnama**?
practice.solution: **Babur** wrote the **Baburnama** himself in **Turkish**; the Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri is Jahangir's memoir; Akbar's story was written for him by Abul Fazl.

practice.q: The **Discovery of India** was written by:
practice.solution: **Nehru** wrote it during his Ahmednagar prison years (1942-46); his other book is **Glimpses of World History**.

practice.q: Who wrote **Hind Swaraj**, the classic statement of his political philosophy?
practice.solution: **Gandhi** wrote **Hind Swaraj** in 1909 aboard a ship from London to South Africa; his autobiography is *My Experiments with Truth*.

practice.q: **Gitanjali**, for which its author received the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1913, is a collection of —
practice.solution: **Gitanjali** ('Song Offerings') is Tagore's collection of poems; he was the **first Asian** to win a Nobel Prize.

practice.q: **Wings of Fire** is the autobiography of:
practice.solution: **Wings of Fire** traces Kalam's journey from Rameswaram to ISRO, DRDO and the Rashtrapati Bhavan.

practice.q: **My Experiments with Truth** is the autobiography of:
practice.solution: Gandhi's autobiography, first published in Gujarati, is ***The Story of My Experiments with Truth***; Mandela's is *Long Walk to Freedom*.

practice.q: The autobiography **A Shot at History** is associated with which sportsperson?
practice.solution: **A Shot at History: My Obsessive Journey to Olympic Gold** - shooter **Abhinav Bindra**, co-written with Rohit Brijnath.

practice.q: Who wrote **Midnight's Children**, winner of the 1981 Booker Prize and later the 'Booker of Bookers'?
practice.solution: **Salman Rushdie's** Midnight's Children (1981) was judged the best Booker winner in 25 and 40 years of the prize.

practice.q: **The Inheritance of Loss**, which won the 2006 Booker Prize, was written by:
practice.solution: **Kiran Desai** won the 2006 Booker for The Inheritance of Loss; her mother **Anita Desai** was shortlisted several times but never won.

practice.q: **War and Peace** was written by the Russian novelist:
practice.solution: **Leo Tolstoy** wrote War and Peace; Dostoevsky wrote Crime and Punishment.

practice.q: Who wrote **Don Quixote**, often called the first modern novel?
practice.solution: **Cervantes** (Spain) wrote Don Quixote; Homer is the ancient Greek author of the Iliad and the Odyssey.

practice.q: **The Republic**, the foundational text of Western political philosophy, was written by:
practice.solution: **Plato's** The Republic discusses justice and the ideal state; Aristotle wrote Politics.

practice.q: The books **Animal Farm** and **Nineteen Eighty-Four** were written by:
practice.solution: **George Orwell** (Eric Blair) wrote both satires of totalitarianism; Huxley wrote Brave New World.

practice.q: The **Ranji Trophy** is associated with which sport?
practice.solution: The **Ranji Trophy** (since 1934) is India's premier first-class cricket championship, named after Ranjitsinhji.

practice.q: The **Sudirman Cup** is a world mixed-team championship of which sport?
practice.solution: **Sudirman Cup** = badminton mixed teams; **Thomas Cup** = men, **Uber Cup** = women.

practice.q: The **Ryder Cup** is a team competition in which sport, contested between the USA and Europe?
practice.solution: The **Ryder Cup** is golf's USA v Europe biennial match; the Davis Cup is tennis's equivalent for nations.

practice.q: The **Swaythling Cup** is awarded in which sport?
practice.solution: The **Swaythling Cup** goes to the men's team champion of world table tennis; the Corbillon Cup is the women's equivalent.

practice.q: The term '**bull's eye**' is associated with which sport?
practice.solution: A **bull's eye** is the centre of the target in archery and shooting events.

practice.q: The terms '**gambit**' and '**castling**' belong to which sport?
practice.solution: A **gambit** is an opening sacrifice, **castling** a king-rook move - both chess terms.

practice.q: '**Birdie**' and '**eagle**', terms for strokes under par, belong to which sport?
practice.solution: **Golf**: one under par = birdie, two under = eagle, one over = bogey.

practice.q: A **water polo** team has how many players in the pool?
practice.solution: **Water polo - seven** a side (six field players plus a goalkeeper). Kabaddi also fields seven.

practice.q: A **rugby union** team fields how many players?
practice.solution: **Rugby union - fifteen** a side; rugby league plays thirteen.

practice.q: Which team sport has exactly **four** players per side?
practice.solution: **Polo - four** mounted players a side. Basketball is five, kabaddi seven, baseball nine.

practice.q: Which Grand Slam tennis tournament is the **oldest**, first played in 1877?
practice.solution: **Wimbledon** (All England Club, London, grass) began in 1877 - the oldest tennis tournament in the world.

practice.q: The first **FIFA World Cup** football tournament (1930) was hosted and won by:
practice.solution: **Uruguay** hosted and won in 1930, beating Argentina in the final; the tournament is held every four years.

practice.q: The first **Cricket World Cup** (1975) was hosted by England. Which team won it?
practice.solution: The **West Indies**, captained by Clive Lloyd, beat Australia in the 1975 final at Lord's.

practice.q: The first modern **Olympic Games** (1896) were held in:
practice.solution: **Athens, 1896** - revived by Pierre de Coubertin; the IOC had been founded in Paris in 1894.

practice.q: The Olympic motto 'Citius, Altius, Fortius' means:
practice.solution: **Citius, Altius, Fortius** = Faster, Higher, Stronger (Latin); 'Communiter' (Together) was added in 2021.

practice.q: The **marathon** race in athletics is run over which distance?
practice.solution: **42.195 km**, fixed from the 1908 London route; the legend traces it to the Greek runner Pheidippides.

practice.q: Who won India's **first individual Olympic medal**, a wrestling bronze at Helsinki 1952?
practice.solution: **K.D. Jadhav** (wrestling, 1952 Helsinki) - India's first individual Olympic medal. Norman Pritchard had won two athletics silvers for India back in 1900.

practice.q: **Neeraj Chopra's** Tokyo 2020 gold medal came in which athletics event?
practice.solution: **Javelin throw** - his winning throw measured **87.58 m**; it was India's second-ever individual Olympic gold.

practice.q: India's first chess **Grandmaster** (1988) is:
practice.solution: **Viswanathan Anand** became India's first GM in 1988; he later won the world championship in multiple formats.

practice.q: Which of the following is the **highest civilian award** of India?
practice.solution: **Bharat Ratna** ('Jewel of India') is the highest civilian award; the Param Vir Chakra is the highest *wartime gallantry* award.

practice.q: The **first woman** to receive the Bharat Ratna was:
practice.solution: **Indira Gandhi** (1971). Mother Teresa received it in 1980; M.S. Subbulakshmi in 1998.

practice.q: The Padma awards, in descending order of precedence, are:
practice.solution: **Padma Vibhushan > Padma Bhushan > Padma Shri**, all instituted in 1954, below the Bharat Ratna.

practice.q: Who was the **first Indian** to win the Nobel Prize in Physics?
practice.solution: **C.V. Raman** (1930) for the Raman effect; Tagore's 1913 prize was in Literature.

practice.q: **Kailash Satyarthi** shared the 2014 Nobel Peace Prize with —
practice.solution: Satyarthi (child rights) shared it with **Malala Yousafzai** (Pakistan) - education for all children.

practice.q: Who is the only person to have won **two Nobel Prizes in different sciences**?
practice.solution: **Marie Curie** - Physics 1903 and Chemistry 1911; the first woman laureate. (Pauling and Bardeen also won two Nobels, but one of theirs was Peace or in the same field.)

practice.q: India's **highest wartime gallantry award** is the:
practice.solution: **Param Vir Chakra** - literally 'wheel of the supreme hero'; the Ashoka Chakra is its peacetime counterpart.

practice.q: The **first Param Vir Chakra** was awarded posthumously to which officer of the 1947-48 Kashmir operations?
practice.solution: **Major Somnath Sharma** (Kumaon Regiment) fell at Badgam, November 1947 - the first PVC.

practice.q: India's **highest award in cinema** is the:
options: National Film Award for Best Feature Film
practice.solution: The **Dadasaheb Phalke Award** (from 1969) honours lifetime contribution to Indian cinema; the first went to Devika Rani.

practice.q: The **Abel Prize**, since 2003 called the 'Nobel of mathematics', is awarded by which country?
practice.solution: **Norway** (by its Academy of Science and Letters) gives the Abel Prize; the Fields Medal is the other great mathematics award.

practice.q: The **Ramon Magsaysay Award**, often called the 'Asian Nobel', is given by which country's foundation?
practice.solution: The **Philippines** (Ramon Magsaysay Award Foundation, Manila), from 1958, in memory of President Magsaysay.

practice.q: The first **Gandhi Peace Prize** (1995), instituted by the Government of India, went to:
practice.solution: **Julius Nyerere**, former President of Tanzania, won the first Gandhi Peace Prize (1995).

practice.q: Who was the **first recipient** of India's highest sporting honour (Khel Ratna), in 1991-92?
practice.solution: Chess world champion **Viswanathan Anand** received the first Rajiv Gandhi Khel Ratna (1991-92); renamed after Major Dhyan Chand in 2021.

practice.q: The **Dhyan Chand Award** is given for —
practice.solution: **Dhyan Chand Award** = lifetime contribution to sport; Dronacharya = coaches; Arjuna = players; MAKA = universities.

practice.q: **Teachers' Day** in India (5 September) is the birth anniversary of:
practice.solution: Dr **S. Radhakrishnan**, philosopher and second President, was born on 5 September 1888; since 1962 the day honours teachers.

practice.q: **National Youth Day** (12 January) marks the birth anniversary of:
practice.solution: **Swami Vivekananda** (born 12 January 1863); the date also opens the National Youth Festival.

practice.q: **Engineers' Day** (15 September) commemorates the birth of which engineer?
practice.solution: Sir **M. Visvesvaraya** (1861), knighted engineer of the Krishna Raja Sagara dam and automatic sluices.

practice.q: **National Doctors' Day** (1 July) honours which physician-statesman?
practice.solution: Dr **Bidhan Chandra Roy**, physician and West Bengal Chief Minister, born and died on 1 July; a Bharat Ratna recipient (1961).

practice.q: **National Technology Day** (11 May) recalls which event of 1998?
practice.solution: Operation Shakti's **Pokhran-II tests** of **11 May 1998**; the day celebrates Indian technology.

practice.q: **Hindi Diwas** is observed on 14 September because on that day in 1949 —
options: Hindi was adopted as the official language of the Union
The Sahitya Akademi was set up
practice.solution: The Constituent Assembly adopted **Hindi in Devanagari script** as the official language of the Union on **14 September 1949** (Article 343).

practice.q: **National Voters' Day** (25 January) marks the founding day of the:
practice.solution: The **Election Commission was constituted on 25 January 1950**; Voters' Day has been observed on the date since 2011.

practice.q: **International Yoga Day** is observed on:
practice.solution: **21 June**, the longest day in the north - first observed in **2015** after India's proposal at the UN (2014).

practice.q: **World Food Day** (16 October) is linked to the founding of which organisation?
practice.solution: The **Food and Agriculture Organization** was founded on **16 October 1945** in Rome, its permanent headquarters city.

practice.q: **Human Rights Day** (10 December) commemorates the adoption in 1948 of the:
practice.solution: The **UDHR** was adopted by the UN General Assembly in Paris on **10 December 1948**.

practice.q: **World Water Day** falls on which date?
practice.solution: **22 March** (since 1993). 22 April is Earth Day; 5 June is Environment Day.

practice.q: **Indian Air Force Day** is observed on —
practice.solution: The **IAF was founded on 8 October 1932**; Army Day - 15 January; Navy Day - 4 December.

practice.q: **Army Day** (15 January) recalls the day in 1949 when:
options: K.M. Cariappa became the first Indian Commander-in-Chief
practice.solution: General **K.M. Cariappa** (later Field Marshal) took over from General Sir Francis Butcher on **15 January 1949**.

practice.q: **Constitution Day (Samvidhan Divas)** is observed on 26 November, the day the Constitution was —
practice.solution: Adopted **26 November 1949**; it **came into force on 26 January 1950**, which is Republic Day.

practice.q: Republic Day is fixed on 26 January to honour the **Purna Swaraj** declaration of independence, first publicly celebrated on 26 January of which year?
practice.solution: The Congress declared Purna Swaraj at its **Lahore session (December 1929)**; the first Independence Day was observed on **26 January 1930**, hence the date for Republic Day.

practice.q: The **national aquatic animal** of India is the:
practice.solution: The **Gangetic river dolphin** was declared national aquatic animal in 2009; the Ganga is the national river (2008).

practice.q: Which of the following is India's **national tree**?
practice.solution: The **banyan** (Ficus benghalensis) - longevity and rootedness; the mango is the national fruit.

practice.q: The **Saka calendar**, used in official gazettes alongside the Gregorian calendar, was adopted in —
practice.solution: Adopted from **22 March 1957** (= 1 Chaitra 1879 Saka) on the Calendar Reform Committee's recommendation.

practice.q: The Indian national flag was adopted by the Constituent Assembly on:
practice.solution: **22 July 1947** - about a fortnight before Independence; the ratio is 3:2.

practice.q: Who designed the present form of the **Indian national flag**?
practice.solution: **Pingali Venkayya** of Andhra, whose design (with Gandhi's suggested additions) became the tricolour.

practice.q: In the national flag, the **navy-blue Ashoka Chakra** stands for —
options: Progress and motion (the wheel of law)
practice.solution: The chakra represents the **wheel of law (dharma)** and constant movement forward; the 24 spokes evoke the hours of the day.

practice.q: *Vande Mataram*, India's national song, is taken from Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay's novel —
practice.solution: ***Anandamath*** (1882); the song was first sung at the 1896 Calcutta session of the Congress.

practice.q: The State Emblem of India is adapted from the Lion Capital of Ashoka at —
practice.solution: The **Sarnath** capital (four lions on an abacus), adopted on 26 January 1950 with the motto Satyameva Jayate.

practice.q: The words **'Satyameva Jayate'** on the state emblem are taken from:
practice.solution: The **Mundaka Upanishad** - 'truth alone triumphs'.

practice.q: Who was the **first woman Speaker** of the Lok Sabha?
practice.solution: **Meira Kumar** (2009-14); Sumitra Mahajan followed her in the chair.

practice.q: The **first Indian woman to reach the summit of Mount Everest** (1984) was:
practice.solution: **Bachendri Pal** (Tata group mountaineer) climbed Everest in May 1984; Santosh Yadav summited twice later.

practice.q: Who was the **first woman President of the Indian National Congress**?
practice.solution: **Annie Besant** presided over the Calcutta session in 1917; **Sarojini Naidu** was the first Indian woman, in 1925 (Kanpur session).

practice.q: India's **first Prime Minister** was:
practice.solution: **Nehru** (1947-64), also the longest-serving Prime Minister; Rajendra Prasad was the first President.

practice.q: The **first Indian satellite**, launched in 1975, was named:
practice.solution: **Aryabhata**, launched (from a Soviet rocket) in 1975 and named after the ancient astronomer.

practice.q: **23 August**, the day Chandrayaan-3 landed near the Moon's south pole (2023), is observed as —
practice.solution: **National Space Day** - the Vikram lander touched down on 23 August 2023, making India the fourth country to soft-land on the Moon.

practice.q: India's **first passenger train** ran in 1853 between:
practice.solution: **16 April 1853** - 34 km from Bombay (Bori Bunder) to Thane; the first railway company had been formed in 1849.

practice.q: Who was the **first Indian to travel into space** (1984)?
practice.solution: Sqn Ldr **Rakesh Sharma** flew on the Soviet Soyuz T-11 in 1984; his reply from orbit - 'saare jahaan se achha'. Ravish Malhotra was his backup.

practice.q: The headquarters of **UNESCO** are in:
practice.solution: **UNESCO - Paris**; UNICEF and UNDP sit at New York; WHO and WTO at Geneva.

practice.q: The **Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO)** is headquartered in:
practice.solution: **Rome** (Italy) - shared with the World Food Programme; UNEP alone is in Nairobi.

practice.q: Which specialised agency of the UN is headquartered in **Nairobi**?
practice.solution: The **UN Environment Programme** - making Nairobi the only UN headquarters city in the Global South.

practice.q: The headquarters of **SAARC** are at:
practice.solution: **SAARC - Kathmandu** (founded 1985); BIMSTEC's secretariat is in Dhaka.

practice.q: The **Asian Development Bank (ADB)** is headquartered at:
practice.solution: **ADB - Manila** (1966). AIIB sits in Beijing and the NDB (BRICS bank) in Shanghai.

practice.q: The **International Olympic Committee (IOC)** is headquartered at:
practice.solution: **Lausanne**, Switzerland - the 'Olympic Capital'; FIFA's HQ is in Zurich.

practice.q: **INTERPOL**, the international police organisation (founded 1923), has its headquarters at:
practice.solution: **INTERPOL - Lyon, France** (it began in Vienna in 1923). The Hague hosts the ICJ and OPCW.

practice.q: The currency of **Bangladesh** is the:
practice.solution: **Taka**. The rupiah belongs to Indonesia; the rupee to India, Pakistan, Nepal and Sri Lanka.

practice.q: The currency of **Myanmar** is the:
practice.solution: **Kyat**. Thailand - baht; Laos - kip; Malaysia - ringgit.

practice.q: The currency of **South Africa** is the:
practice.solution: **Rand**. Nigeria - naira; Kenya - shilling; Botswana - pula.

practice.q: Which country's currency is the **real**?
practice.solution: **Brazil** uses the real; Mexico and Argentina use pesos; Chile the Chilean peso.

practice.q: The **Diet** is the national legislature of:
practice.solution: Japan's parliament is the **Diet** (House of Representatives + House of Councillors); China's is the National People's Congress.

practice.q: The parliament of **Iran** is known as the:
practice.solution: Iran's parliament is the **Majlis**; Pakistan's federal legislature is the Majlis-e-Shoora.

practice.q: The **Folketing** is the parliament of which country?
practice.solution: **Denmark - Folketing**; Norway - Storting; Sweden - Riksdag.

practice.q: The lower house of Russia's Federal Assembly is called the:
practice.solution: The **State Duma** is the lower house; the Federation Council is the upper house. (Gosplan was the Soviet planning body.)

practice.q: The **World Health Organization** was established in:
practice.solution: **WHO - 7 April 1948** (hence World Health Day); it sits in Geneva.

practice.q: **ASEAN**, the association of South-East Asian nations, was founded in 1967 at:
practice.solution: Founded at **Bangkok** by the five original members (Indonesia, Malaysia, Philippines, Singapore, Thailand); its headquarters are in **Jakarta**.

practice.q: Which pair of organisations was created together at the **Bretton Woods Conference** (1944)?
practice.solution: The **Bretton Woods twins** - the IMF and the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (now the World Bank), both seated at Washington DC.
